html:
Indian Territory was the land west of Arkansas that the United States set aside for Native American nations it moved out of the east, from the 1830s until it became part of the state of Oklahoma in 1907.

Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 the US forced the southeastern nations west on the Trail of Tears. The Choctaw, Cherokee, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole rebuilt their nations there, with written constitutions, courts, schools and newspapers. Many of their leaders sided with the Confederacy in the Civil War, and in 1866 the US made them give up the western half of their lands.

That western land was then used to settle more nations moved from the Plains and the Midwest: the Pawnee, Osage, Kaw, Ponca, Sac and Fox, Cheyenne and Arapaho, and others. In 1889 the US opened unassigned land to white settlers in a land run, and in 1890 it made the west into Oklahoma Territory. Under the Dawes Act and later laws, tribal land was cut into private plots and the "surplus" sold. In 1907 the two territories were joined as the state of Oklahoma, which is still home to dozens of tribal nations.
